title: We Only Know Her as Mei
body_text: If you haven’t read this story yet, you should. It’s an excellent piece of journalism from the team here at Science and at Retraction Watch, and it reveals a previously unreported death from an attempt at gene therapy in China last year. We know where it happened (Xinhua Hospital) and we know the principal investigator for the trial (Zilong Qiu). But the six-year-old girl who was killed we know only as Mei. She was born with a rare mutation leading to Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome. It’s a T-for-C switch in the sequence of the CHD3 gene (chromodomain helicase DNA binding protein 3), and that is involved in a histone deacetylase complex for chromatin remodeling and transcription. Mutations in this gene vary in the severity of their phenotype, but these typically include developmental delays, eventual intellectual disability (with language and speech effects), and more. Mei herself appears to have been at the milder end of this diagnosis, but nonetheless with unmistakeable signs. Since this is a single base residue effect, this is the sort of condition that is in theory a candidate for base editing, and one would think that the earlier this can be accomplished, the better the eventual outcome would be. This sort of intervention was famously accomplished last year in Philadelphia with “Baby KJ”, who was born with a defect in the gene for carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1. This disrupts the metabolic nitrogen handling and recycling system, resulting in major problems with urea and ammonia levels, and when it is present from birth (as was the case with KJ) it leads to severe consequences and often an early death. (His multiple rounds of treatment seems to have definitely improved his condition, but he's being watched closely to see if more rounds will be needed). As the Science story details, there are a number of similarities and also a number of key differences in the cases of Mei and KJ. Start with the underlying conditions: KJ’s was certain to result in major damage to all his organs (including the brain), even with treatment with various nitrogen-scavenging drugs. Mei’s, on the other hand, had no excess risk of death, but would certainly result in functional impairment to some degree. It’s an open question what her prognosis would have been had she survived - no one has ever corrected something like a CHD3 impairment, and whether six years of age was too late to help or still well within range of therapeutic effect is of course unknown. Another difference is the site of treatment. KJ’s disease needed to be corrected in the liver, which is why he was such a good candidate for a first-in-human attempt like this. All of the known methods to apply gene therapies are going to go right to the liver anyway if infused into the general circulation. But Mei’s condition would require injection in the cerebrospinal fluid. And yet another difference was the vector used for the base-editing CRISPR constructs. KJ’s was done by mRNA, packaged in lipid nanoparticle, while Mei’s was done with a viral vector (AAV9). The payload needed was too large to be put into one package with this virus, so a split dual-vector strategy was used where successful editing would take place only in those cells that were infected with both virus forms. Whether or not this would achieve enough coverage to have a therapeutic effect was also unknown. Qiu’s team had successfully edited CHD3 in mice, but that was with a single vector that itself could cross the rodent blood-brain barrier. The human test would have to be very different. A study had been done in macaque monkeys as well, but as you’ll see in the Science article, there are disagreements about how well it worked. And what was for sure was that all the monkeys treated had shown signs of liver damage, and kidney damage at the highest dose. Those differences appears to have been what killed Mei (I refuse to use passive verb constructions here). She developed a fever after the injection of the viral vectors into her spine (which was expected) but then showed signs of kidney trouble. And it appears to have been thrombotic microangiopathy in the kidney tissue that was the proximal cause of death, about five days after the treatment. Reading the details in the article, it is hard to come to any other conclusion other than that this attempt moved too quickly, with too little attention to what could go wrong. Mei’s parents say that they were never told that death was even possible due to the treatment, and that’s just irresponsible, since a first-in-human intervention of this sort is always going to run that risk. I feel certain that KJ's parents were given such information (and that they weighed this along with the likelihood of death and damage without such an intervention). There’s more. That paper from Qiu’s group linked above appears to have been substantially revised during its publication process at Nature, with many experiments from the original manuscript redone, no mention of the kidney and liver problems in the primate study, and all mention of Mei and her parents removed (even though they had helped to fund this work out of their own pockets). None of the referees for the paper were aware that this work had led to a human patient being dosed, and none of them were of course aware that it had killed her within days. For now, the journal seems to be taking the position that these issues should be handled by the university hospital (update: see below), and the university seems to be taking the position that no one is going to be really disciplined for this at all. In fact, the parents have been told by the university that the Nature paper “bears no relation to the experiments you funded”, which is of course outrageous. So I’m glad that Science and Retraction Watch have dragged this story into the light. The gene-therapy community needs to know about it as a cautionary tale, just as much as the Jesse Gelsinger gene therapy death in 1999. And justice is owed to a family, and to the memory of a six-year-old girl who we know only as Mei. Update: I've heard from people at Nature about this post, and they have several comments. The first is that the journal (and its editors and reviewers) had no information that a human trial was going to take place (or had!) because there was no mention of any such thing in any version of the manuscript. That's absolutely a fair point, and I'm glad to emphasize it. They also note that since the paper was a preclinical study (covering cells, mice, and primate studies) that it contained no information about toxicological effects, and that nothing of this short was ever communicated to the journal. Fair as well! And they also want to note that the journal is taking this seriously, and that they are investigating concerns around the paper and plan to take action once the investigation is complete. That's the right course of action, and I'm glad to hear it, because the information I had about their response did not go that far. It appears that they will have a lot to investigate, considering the numerous changes that seem to have been made between different version of the paper (such as the removal of the human sequence data from the girl and her parents, and what appear to be completely re-done rodent experiments). There is of course no way to tell what authors have deliberately left out of a manuscript, though - and in this case what they appear to have left out was the crucial information that the primate study (whose results they show in the paper) also showed unmistakeable signs of toxicity in the animals, and - even worse - that they planned to give this treatment to a six-year-old girl anyway. That part is not Nature's problem. But it should be someone's.
